newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan not mulling stock-boosting steps - govt source.
newsitem.headline: Japan not mulling stock-boosting steps - govt source.

text.p: The Japanese government is not considering any short-term measures to boost share prices at the moment, as the share plunge is unlikely to affect the real economy immediately, a government source said on Tuesday.
"I don't think there are talks going on within the government about (short-term) measures to boost stock prices at the moment," the source, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

The government is more worried about the impact of the stock price fall on consumer and corporate sentiment. But such effects will be felt over a longer period of time, so there is no urgency in addressing the stock market woes, he said.

The Tokyo stock market was briefly buoyed earlier on Tuesday by rumours that the authorities were poised to announce rescue measures for sagging share prices, but the rumours were later denied by a Finance Ministry official.

Meanwhile, the government will work to implement its extra budget for this fiscal year and the full state budget for the next fiscal year without delay. It will also work to carry out planned deregulation measures, the source said.

Many people are worried that the fall in Tokyo share prices will erode unrealised profits on shares owned by banks, which would make it difficult for the banks to meet capital adequacy requirements. This could lead banks to reduce their total assets by reducing lendings.
The source said that there was not much corporate demand for funds to begin with and that big firms are using what they have at hand for capital investment.

Although there are worries that sentiment may worsen to the point where it starts affecting corporate capital investment, he said companies are likely to wait until the last moment, say around March, before finalising their investment plans for the next fiscal year starting in April.

Concerning the recent weakness of the yen against the dollar, the government holds the view that excessive volatility is undesirable, but a gradual fall in the value of the yen is not something to be terribly worried about, he said.
He added that Japanese companies had wanted a further weakening of the yen when it was still at a rate of around 105 yen to the dollar, but there had not been many complaints at the current level.
The depreciation of the yen has not yet affected domestic prices in a way to raise fears of inflation, the source said.
The government has said in its monthly economic report that a recent fall in prices has stopped.
Separately, a senior Economic Planning Agency (EPA) official said that the current situation did not warrant macro-economic steps to support share prices, such as making changes in interest rates.
The senior EPA official added that he did not think the negative impact of the weaker yen on the economy was prominent yet, as there are more exporters among Japanese companies than importers.
